buckets.title: Vector addition, subtraction and orientation
buckets.badge_reason: Direction and operand order must survive several representations; river-crossing constraints additionally require component cancellation before magnitude work.

conventions.statement: Treat subtraction order as part of the requested directed result; swapping the order reverses orientation rather than merely changing notation.

scope.covers: Unit-direction normalisation, vector addition/decomposition with signed-component cancellation, subtraction-order orientation, and qualitative cross-product orientation.
excluded: General three-dimensional vector algebra beyond the existing matrix intent.

capabilities.action: Separate a nonzero vector's direction from its magnitude by constructing or interpreting the unit vector along it.
capabilities.success_criterion: Given two nonzero vectors or one vector and its magnitude, explain that dividing by the magnitude produces a magnitude-one vector in the same direction, and use that direction-only representation without confusing equal magnitudes with equal vectors.

capabilities.action: Compose vectors by tail-to-head or signed components and resolve a vector along declared perpendicular axes, including choosing one component to cancel a specified resultant component.
capabilities.success_criterion: Given two directed quantities or a resultant-direction constraint, declare axes, preserve component signs, add corresponding components, impose any required cancellation, and check the same resultant geometrically.

capabilities.action: Distinguish the orientation of A minus B from B minus A.
capabilities.success_criterion: State that swapping the subtraction order reverses the directed result.

capabilities.action: Determine the perpendicular direction of the cross product for an ordered pair of nonparallel vectors and predict how swapping the order or making the vectors parallel changes the result.
capabilities.success_criterion: For an oriented input plane, give the two opposite cross-product directions for A cross B and B cross A, and identify the parallel-input case as zero without using a determinant calculation.

microtopics.title: Unit direction keeps orientation and removes size
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners often treat an arrow's length as inseparable from the directed quantity and therefore miss why differently sized parallel vectors can share one direction-only representation.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish a vector from its magnitude.
Can divide a nonzero quantity by its own positive magnitude.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Normalising a nonzero vector removes its original size but preserves its direction, so different positive multiples in one direction share the same unit-direction vector.

teaching_path.action: Draw two arrows from the same start, one three times as long as the other, with both pointing in exactly the same direction.
teaching_path.why_valid: Holding direction fixed while changing only length separates directional information from magnitude.
teaching_path.output: short arrow: magnitude L, long arrow: magnitude 3L, both with the same direction.

teaching_path.action: Scale each nonzero arrow by the reciprocal of its own magnitude.
teaching_path.why_valid: Multiplying a vector by a positive scalar changes its magnitude by that factor without reversing its direction.
teaching_path.output: short/L and long/(3L) both have magnitude 1 and point the same way.

teaching_path.action: Multiply the direction-only arrow back by L and by 3L and compare with the two original arrows.
teaching_path.why_valid: Reconstruction shows that one unit direction plus a scalar magnitude recovers either original directed quantity.
teaching_path.output: L times the unit direction recovers the short arrow; 3L times it recovers the long arrow.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A unit vector is a different direction invented by making the arrow one unit long.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two nonzero arrows point northeast; one is three times longer. After each is normalised, should the two direction-only arrows point differently?
misconceptions.repair: Keep the direction fixed while dividing each arrow by its own positive magnitude. Only the size is removed; the direction is preserved.

exit_task.prompt: Vector A points southwest with magnitude 6 units. Vector B points southwest with magnitude 2 units. Compare the unit-direction vectors along A and B, and state how A can be reconstructed from its unit direction.

answer.summary: The two unit-direction vectors are the same because A and B point in the same direction. A is 6 times that unit-direction vector.
reasoning: Normalising divides each nonzero vector by its positive magnitude.
Positive scaling does not reverse direction.
Both vectors therefore reduce to the same magnitude-one direction.
Multiplying that unit direction by 6 reconstructs A.
answer.check: The reconstructed arrow must point southwest and have magnitude 6.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: Only the given magnitude 6 is reused as the reconstruction scale; no derived measurement is asserted.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created migration of the existing R1 matrix intent. The imported candidate packet was consulted only as non-authoritative input; no external review authority is claimed.

predict.prompt: Two arrows point in exactly the same direction, but one is three times longer. If each is divided by its own magnitude, do the results still differ?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Both become magnitude-one arrows in the same direction.

attempt.produces: A before/after sketch for the two same-direction arrows, with original magnitudes labelled and both normalised results shown at equal unit length.

rubric.criterion: The normalised arrows preserve the original common direction.
Both normalised arrows have magnitude one.
rubric.evidence_of: Using the vector's own positive magnitude as the scale factor.

accepted: Both original arrows reduce to the same magnitude-one arrow pointing in their common direction.
rejected: The longer arrow keeps a longer unit vector, which means its magnitude was not actually removed.

route.ask: What did we hold fixed when drawing the two original arrows?
route.why_this_ask: It isolates direction as shared information.

route.ask: What positive factor makes each arrow's magnitude become one?
route.why_this_ask: The learner derives normalisation from scaling rather than memorising notation.

route.ask: How would you recover either original arrow from the shared unit direction?

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path demonstrates the scale change; the elicitation route starts from two unequal lengths and makes the learner identify what survives normalisation.

boundary_test.prompt: Can the zero vector be normalised by dividing by its magnitude?
boundary_test.answer: No. Its magnitude is zero, so division by its magnitude is undefined and there is no unique direction to preserve.
boundary_test.confirms: The unit-direction construction applies only to nonzero vectors.

microtopics.title: Add vectors by components and engineer component cancellation
microtopics.badge_reason: The difficult move is not arithmetic but preserving direction: learners often add magnitudes, drop signs, or miss that a required resultant direction is a component constraint.
entry_assumptions: Can read signed vector components against declared axes.
Can interpret a unit direction separately from magnitude.
Can obtain a hypotenuse from perpendicular leg lengths through the declared Mathematics bridge.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Vector addition is a directional ledger: corresponding signed components add independently, and a required resultant direction can be enforced by making the unwanted component sum to zero.

teaching_path.action: Declare perpendicular positive axes and write each input vector as signed horizontal and vertical parts before combining anything.
teaching_path.why_valid: A declared axis system makes direction explicit and prevents a speed or magnitude from silently replacing a directed quantity.
teaching_path.output: A=(A_x,A_y), B=(B_x,B_y), with the signs read from the declared axes.

teaching_path.action: Place the second arrow tail-to-head with the first and, in parallel, add corresponding signed parts.
teaching_path.why_valid: Tail-to-head translation preserves each vector, while addition along independent perpendicular axes gives the same endpoint displacement.
teaching_path.output: R=A+B=(A_x+B_x, A_y+B_y), matching the arrow from the first tail to the final head.

teaching_path.action: When the requested resultant must have no motion along one axis, set that resultant part to zero and solve the cancellation condition before finding any magnitude.
teaching_path.why_valid: A direction constraint such as 'directly opposite' or 'straight across' is equivalent to saying the unwanted signed component of the resultant is zero.
teaching_path.output: for a zero horizontal resultant: A_x+B_x=0, so one input must supply the equal-and-opposite horizontal part.

teaching_path.action: Check the signed-component result against the tail-to-head diagram and, for perpendicular resultant parts, use the right-triangle bridge only after the signs and cancellation are settled.
teaching_path.why_valid: The diagram checks direction and the bridge checks magnitude; agreement between representations catches dropped signs and magnitude-only addition.
teaching_path.output: direction agrees with the signed parts; magnitude is computed from the nonnegative leg lengths only when needed.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The magnitude of A plus B is always the sum of the two input magnitudes.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A 5-unit vector points east and another 5-unit vector points west. What is the resultant vector?
misconceptions.repair: Add directed components, not magnitudes. Equal and opposite components cancel, so the resultant is zero.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If the desired path is straight across a river, the swimmer should simply aim straight across relative to the water.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A current adds an eastward component. What must the swimmer's water-relative velocity contribute horizontally if the ground-relative path must have zero east-west component?
misconceptions.repair: Translate the path constraint into a component equation: the swimmer must supply an equal westward component so the east-west resultant is zero.

exit_task.prompt: A river current is 3 units/s east. A swimmer can move at 5 units/s relative to the water and wants the ground-relative path to be due north. What west-east component must the swimmer choose, and what northward component then remains?

answer.summary: The swimmer must contribute 3 units/s west so the horizontal parts cancel. With total swimmer-relative speed 5, the remaining northward part is 4 units/s.
reasoning: Take east as positive horizontal and north as positive vertical.
The current contributes +3 horizontally, so a due-north resultant requires swimmer horizontal component -3.
The swimmer-relative speed 5 is the hypotenuse of perpendicular component lengths 3 and the unknown northward part.
The right-triangle relation gives the northward part sqrt(5^2-3^2)=4.
answer.check: Horizontal ground-relative component: +3 + (-3)=0; swimmer component magnitude: sqrt(3^2+4^2)=5.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The 3-4-5 check is an author-created illustrative verification, not a sourced measurement.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created completion of the existing R2 matrix intent, specifically activated by the owner-supplied river-crossing demand. The external NEETPrep items remain transient and are not copied into canonical content.

predict.prompt: A current carries 3 units/s east. If a swimmer wants the ground-relative path to have no east-west motion, what must be true of the swimmer's horizontal part?
predict.defensible_answer: It must be 3 units/s west so the horizontal parts sum to zero.

attempt.produces: A declared-axis component ledger for current + swimmer = ground result, with the unwanted component set to zero before any magnitude calculation.

rubric.criterion: Axes and signs are declared before addition.
rubric.evidence_of: Preserving direction rather than adding bare magnitudes.

rubric.criterion: The required path direction is translated into a zero-component equation.
rubric.evidence_of: Using the physical constraint to determine cancellation.

rubric.criterion: A geometric/tail-to-head check agrees with the component result.
rubric.evidence_of: Reconciling two representations of the same vector sum.

accepted: east positive: current=(3,0), swimmer=(-3,v), result=(0,v); then determine v only if the swimmer's speed is needed.
rejected: Add 3 to 5 because both are speeds, without representing their directions.

route.ask: Which direction should be positive on each axis, and what signed pair does each input have?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents scalar-only reasoning before the operation begins.

route.ask: What component of the required ground result must be zero?
route.why_this_ask: It converts wording such as 'directly opposite' into a precise constraint.

route.ask: Which input component must cancel the current's unwanted part?
route.why_this_ask: The learner solves the directional condition before touching magnitude.

route.ask: Does the tail-to-head endpoint point in the same direction as the component sum?
route.why_this_ask: A second representation catches sign and order mistakes.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path shows both geometric and component addition; the elicitation route begins with the desired direction and makes the learner derive the cancellation equation.

boundary_test.prompt: If two equal vectors point in exactly opposite directions, what do the component sum and tail-to-head construction both give?
boundary_test.answer: The zero vector. Every signed component cancels, and the final head returns to the starting point.
boundary_test.confirms: Magnitude addition is only valid in special same-direction cases; vector addition preserves orientation.

microtopics.title: Operand order reverses a subtraction result
microtopics.badge_reason: The construction may already be familiar, but learners can still preserve the same arrow direction after swapping the words.
entry_assumptions: Can construct one graphical subtraction by reversing the second arrow before tail-to-head addition.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Swapping which directed quantity comes first in a subtraction reverses the result's direction while leaving its length unchanged.

teaching_path.action: Write two ordered requests for the same pair: A minus B, then B minus A.
teaching_path.why_valid: Keeping the pair fixed isolates order as the only change.
teaching_path.output: case 1: A minus B.  case 2: B minus A.

teaching_path.action: For A minus B, follow A and then the reversed B arrow using the already-learned subtraction construction.
teaching_path.why_valid: The prerequisite construction gives a directed result for the stated order without introducing a new rule.
teaching_path.output: A - B -> one completed arrow from the common start to the construction endpoint.

teaching_path.action: Repeat with the order swapped and place both completed arrows from the same start for comparison.
teaching_path.why_valid: Only the order changed, so direct superposition exposes what order does to orientation.
teaching_path.output: B minus A: same drawn length as the first result, pointing exactly the opposite way.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Vector subtraction is commutative in the same way as vector addition.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If A minus B points east, must B minus A point east too?
misconceptions.repair: Keep the same two inputs, swap only their order, and compare the two completed arrows from one start; the second points opposite the first.

exit_task.prompt: Two labelled arrows A and B are shown, and a completed construction for A minus B points southeast. Without recalculating its length, describe the direction of B minus A and explain the check you used.

answer.summary: B minus A points northwest: exactly opposite to the shown result, with the same length.
reasoning: The two requests use the same pair and differ only in order.
Swapping the order swaps which arrow is reversed in the known construction.
Placing both results from one start makes the second point opposite the first.
answer.check: Swap the labels again; the direction must return to southeast without changing the length.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer asserts no computed magnitude. It checks the qualitative reversal caused by swapping operand order.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created distinction layered on the existing graphical-subtraction capability. The candidate packet was consulted as non-authoritative input; no packet claim is promoted.

predict.prompt: A minus B has already been drawn pointing southeast. Before drawing anything else, where do you expect B minus A to point?
predict.defensible_answer: Northwest, because swapping the order reverses the completed directed result while keeping its length.

attempt.produces: A second arrow, drawn from the same start as the first, showing the predicted direction for B minus A plus one sentence naming what changed.

rubric.criterion: The second arrow points exactly opposite the first.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating operand order as directional information.

rubric.criterion: The explanation says order changed while the input pair stayed fixed.
rubric.evidence_of: Isolating the cause of the reversal instead of appealing to a memorized sign change.

accepted: A northwest arrow from the same start, the same length as the southeast arrow, with the note 'same pair; order swapped, so direction reverses.'
rejected: Another southeast arrow labelled B minus A. This treats subtraction as if swapping operands left the directed result unchanged.

route.ask: Which of the two original arrows is second in A minus B, and what does the construction do to that second arrow?
route.why_this_ask: It reconnects the new order question to the already-owned graphical construction.

route.ask: Now make B the first quantity. Which arrow is second this time?
route.why_this_ask: The learner has to identify the single structural change before seeing the result.

route.ask: Draw the swapped-order result from the same start as the first. Which way does it point relative to the first?
route.why_this_ask: Superposition turns the order change into a visible orientation change.

route.ask: What stayed unchanged when the order swapped?
route.why_this_ask: Naming the unchanged length prevents the learner from treating reversal as an unrelated second calculation.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path demonstrates both orders. The learner route begins with a prediction from one completed order, then reconstructs the second and uses superposition to test the prediction.

boundary_test.prompt: Suppose A and B are identical arrows. What do both subtraction orders produce, and what happens to the idea of an opposite direction?
boundary_test.answer: Both give the zero result. Its length is zero, so there is no direction to reverse.
boundary_test.confirms: The reversal statement applies to a directed nonzero result; the zero case is the limiting boundary.

microtopics.title: Ordered cross-product direction
microtopics.badge_reason: The operation is order-sensitive in a way ordinary addition is not; learners can remember 'perpendicular' yet still point the result to the wrong side of the input plane.
entry_assumptions: Can preserve operand order in a directed vector operation.
Can distinguish the plane containing two nonparallel input vectors from a direction perpendicular to that plane.
microtopics.inferential_jump: For two nonparallel vectors, the ordered cross product points perpendicular to their plane; swapping the operand order reverses that direction, while parallel inputs give zero.

teaching_path.action: Draw A and B from one start in the same plane and label the order A first, B second.
teaching_path.why_valid: The ordered pair, not just the two unlabeled arrows, determines which of the two perpendicular directions is selected.
teaching_path.output: one oriented input plane with a declared first and second vector.

teaching_path.action: Use the conventional right-hand orientation: align fingers with the first vector and curl toward the second through the smaller angle; the thumb selects the perpendicular direction.
teaching_path.why_valid: This orientation convention assigns one of the two opposite perpendicular directions consistently to the ordered pair.
teaching_path.output: A cross B is assigned to one side of the input plane.

teaching_path.action: Swap the labels so B is first and A is second, repeat the orientation check, and compare the two results.
teaching_path.why_valid: The same input plane is held fixed while only order changes, isolating the sign reversal caused by anti-commutativity.
teaching_path.output: B cross A points to the opposite side of the same input plane.

teaching_path.action: Rotate B until it becomes parallel to A and observe the limiting case.
teaching_path.why_valid: With no swept area between parallel directions, the cross-product magnitude is zero, so no nonzero perpendicular arrow remains.
teaching_path.output: parallel inputs give the zero vector; perpendicular fixed-magnitude inputs give the largest cross-product magnitude.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Swapping A and B leaves the cross-product direction unchanged because the same two vectors are used.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If A cross B points out of the page, where must B cross A point?
misconceptions.repair: Keep the plane fixed and reverse only the operand order; the selected perpendicular direction flips to the opposite side.

exit_task.prompt: Take a right-handed page coordinate system with east as +x and north as +y. A points east and B points north. State the directions of A cross B and B cross A, then state what happens if B is rotated until it also points east.

answer.summary: A cross B points +z (out of the page), B cross A points -z (into the page), and parallel eastward inputs give the zero vector.
reasoning: The ordered east-to-north turn selects +z under the declared orientation convention.
Swapping the order reverses the perpendicular direction.
Parallel inputs have zero cross-product magnitude.
answer.check: Swapping the operands twice must return the original direction; making the included angle zero must eliminate the nonzero perpendicular result.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The task checks qualitative orientation and the parallel zero case; it does not ask for a computed magnitude.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created completion of the already-committed R4 matrix skeleton. It does not add a new matrix or new learner product and claims no independent scientific review.

predict.prompt: A cross B points out of the page. Without redrawing the vectors, what direction should B cross A point?
predict.defensible_answer: Into the page: swapping the ordered pair reverses the perpendicular direction.

attempt.produces: Two side-by-side ordered-pair sketches for A cross B and B cross A, with opposite perpendicular arrows and a one-sentence parallel-input boundary case.

rubric.criterion: The two operand orders produce opposite perpendicular directions.
rubric.evidence_of: Preserving order in the cross product.

rubric.criterion: Parallel inputs are identified as a zero-result case.
rubric.evidence_of: Understanding the orientation result together with its magnitude boundary.

accepted: A×B points to one side of the plane; B×A points to the other; if A and B are parallel the result is zero.
rejected: Both orders point to the same side because the input vectors are unchanged.

route.ask: What stayed fixed when we changed A cross B into B cross A?
route.why_this_ask: It isolates operand order as the only changed feature.

route.ask: Repeat the same orientation convention with the new first vector. Which side of the plane is selected?
route.why_this_ask: The learner reconstructs the reversal rather than memorising a minus sign.

route.ask: What result is left when the two input directions become parallel?
route.why_this_ask: The zero boundary checks that the learner is not treating perpendicular direction as automatic for every pair.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path states the orientation convention first; the elicitation route starts from a known A cross B direction and asks the learner to predict the swapped-order and parallel cases.

boundary_test.prompt: If either input vector is the zero vector, can the cross product have a nonzero perpendicular result?
boundary_test.answer: No. Its magnitude is zero, so the cross product is the zero vector.
boundary_test.confirms: A direction convention does not create a nonzero result when the magnitude condition collapses.
